title: Segment and Fenwick Trees
tagline: Range queries and point updates in O(log n) — the workhorses of competitive programming and time-series analytics.

sections.content:
Two classic operations on arrays are expensive with naive approaches: **range queries** ("what is the sum/min/max of elements from index l to r?") and **point updates** ("change the value at index i"). A brute-force range sum costs O(n); a prefix-sum array answers range sums in O(1) but cannot handle updates (rebuilding the prefix sum after each update costs O(n)).

**Segment trees** and **Fenwick trees** (also called Binary Indexed Trees or BITs) both achieve O(log n) for both queries and updates — a dramatic improvement over the brute-force O(n). The trade-off is O(n) space and O(n) build time. Segment trees are more general — they support range minimum, maximum, GCD, and lazy-propagation range updates — while Fenwick trees are simpler to code and faster in practice for prefix-sum problems. Both are foundational in competitive programming, real-time analytics, and computational geometry.

sections.title: A Company Org Chart with Pre-computed Totals
sections.content:
Imagine a company org chart where every manager knows the **total sales for their entire team**, not just their direct reports. The CEO knows the company total; each VP knows their division total; each director knows their department total — down to individual salespeople at the leaves.

When you want **total sales for the engineering division** you ask the VP of Engineering: one query, instant answer. When a salesperson's number changes, only their manager, their manager's manager, and so on up to the CEO need to update their totals — O(log n) updates. This is exactly how a segment tree works: internal nodes cache aggregated values over their subtree's range, so any range query decomposes into at most O(log n) pre-computed cache reads, and any single update propagates up O(log n) ancestors.

**Segment Tree** is a complete binary tree where each leaf stores one array element and each internal node stores an aggregate (sum, min, max, etc.) over its range. For an array of n elements the tree has at most 4n nodes and is stored in an array using 1-indexed arithmetic (left child = 2i, right child = 2i+1).

**Build** fills the tree bottom-up in O(n). **Query(l, r)** recursively splits the query range: if the current node's range falls entirely inside [l, r], return its cached value; if entirely outside, return an identity (0 for sum, ∞ for min); otherwise recurse on both children and combine. At most 4 log n nodes are visited — O(log n) time. **Update(i, val)** walks from the root to leaf i, updates the leaf, and fixes all ancestors on the way back — O(log n).

**Lazy propagation** extends the segment tree to support **range updates** ("add 5 to every element between index 3 and 7"): a lazy tag at each node defers the actual update until the node is needed, keeping range-update time at O(log n) rather than O(n).

**Fenwick Tree (Binary Indexed Tree)** exploits a bit trick: the number of elements each `bit[i]` is responsible for equals the value of the lowest set bit of i. `update(i, delta)` adds delta and then propagates up by repeatedly adding the lowest set bit: `i += i & (-i)`. `query(i)` sums prefix [1..i] by repeatedly subtracting the lowest set bit: `i -= i & (-i)`. Range sum [l, r] = `query(r) - query(l-1)`. Both operations are O(log n) with extremely small constants — Fenwick trees are often 3–4× faster in practice than segment trees for pure prefix-sum problems.

sections.caption: Segment tree query(2,5): nodes fully inside the range return their cached value; nodes outside return 0. Only O(log n) nodes are visited.

sections.label: Runtime
sections.explanation: The segment tree stores 4n nodes (worst-case allocation). Queries return 0 for ranges fully outside — the identity for sum. The Fenwick tree's `i & (-i)` isolates the lowest set bit: for i=6 (binary 110), `6 & -6 = 2`, so bit[6] covers indices 5–6. The trick is elegant but requires 1-indexed arrays.

sections.label: Concept
sections.explanation: Swapping `+` for `Math.min` converts the sum segment tree into an RMQ tree with no other changes — demonstrating the generality of the segment tree pattern. The identity element changes from 0 (sum) to Infinity (min). Sparse tables achieve O(1) range minimum queries but are read-only (no updates) — use them for static arrays.

sections.content: **Choose a Fenwick tree when you only need prefix sums with point updates — it is half the code and 3× faster than a segment tree.** Choose a segment tree when you need: range minimum/maximum, custom aggregation (GCD, XOR), or range updates via lazy propagation. When the array is static (no updates) and you need O(1) range minimum, use a sparse table instead — it uses O(n log n) space but answers queries with two precomputed lookups.

items: Segment trees and Fenwick trees both answer range queries and support point updates in O(log n) — far better than the O(n) naive approach or the O(n) rebuild cost of prefix sums.
A segment tree is a complete binary tree where each node stores an aggregate over its range; build is O(n), query and update are O(log n).
Lazy propagation extends segment trees to support range updates (e.g. add 5 to all elements in [l, r]) in O(log n) by deferring work until a node is actually queried.
A Fenwick tree (BIT) uses the lowest-set-bit trick `i & (-i)` to maintain prefix sums; it is simpler, faster, and uses less memory than a segment tree for prefix-sum-only problems.
Segment trees generalise to any associative operation (sum, min, max, GCD, XOR); Fenwick trees are typically limited to operations with an efficient inverse (sum, XOR).

quiz.question: What is the time complexity of a range sum query on a segment tree?
options: O(log n)
O(n)
O(n log n)
quiz.explanation: A segment tree query visits at most 4 log n nodes — at each level of the tree it touches at most 4 nodes (2 at the boundaries of the query range). The dominant term is O(log n).

quiz.question: Why can a prefix-sum array not efficiently support point updates?
options: Prefix sums cannot represent negative numbers
Updating one element requires recomputing all prefix sums to the right — O(n) work
Prefix sums do not support range minimum queries
Prefix sums require O(n log n) space
quiz.explanation: A prefix sum array stores `P[i] = arr[0] + arr[1] + ... + arr[i]`. Changing arr[k] invalidates P[k], P[k+1], ..., P[n-1] — all n-k entries must be updated. This makes prefix sums efficient only for static arrays.

quiz.question: What does `i & (-i)` compute for a Fenwick tree index i?
options: The parent of node i
The lowest set bit of i — the number of elements bit[i] is responsible for
The total number of elements in the tree
The index of the right sibling of node i
quiz.explanation: In two's complement, `-i` flips all bits of i and adds 1, which isolates the lowest set bit. For i=6 (binary 110), `6 & -6 = 2 (010)`, meaning bit[6] covers 2 elements (indices 5–6). This bit trick is the core of all Fenwick tree navigation.

quiz.question: What does lazy propagation add to a segment tree?
options: O(1) point updates by skipping ancestor updates
Support for range updates (e.g. add delta to all elements in [l, r]) in O(log n) by deferring updates until a node is queried
O(1) range queries by caching the last result
Ability to store two aggregates per node
quiz.explanation: Without lazy propagation, a range update (add delta to every element in [l, r]) would require visiting all O(n) leaves. Lazy tags mark a node as having a pending update that has not yet been pushed to its children. When a node with a lazy tag is queried or updated, the tag is first applied to the children — keeping all operations at O(log n).

quiz.question: A Fenwick tree is built for the array [3, 1, 4, 1, 5]. What is `query(3)` (prefix sum of first 3 elements, 1-indexed)?
quiz.explanation: The first 3 elements (1-indexed) are 3, 1, 4. Their sum is 3+1+4 = 8. The Fenwick query(3) follows: bit[3] covers index 3 only → 4; then 3 - (3 & -3) = 3-1 = 2; bit[2] covers indices 1–2 → 3+1=4; then 2-2=0, stop. 4+4 = 8.

quiz.question: Which operation is NOT efficiently supported by a standard Fenwick tree?
options: Prefix sum query in O(log n)
Point update (add delta to one element) in O(log n)
Range minimum query (find the minimum in [l, r]) in O(log n)
Range sum query [l, r] in O(log n)
quiz.explanation: Fenwick trees exploit the fact that subtraction is the inverse of addition, enabling prefix-sum decomposition. Minimum has no efficient inverse — you cannot compute min(l, r) from two prefix minimums. For range minimum queries, use a segment tree or sparse table.

quiz.question: How many nodes does a segment tree array need for an input array of size n?
options: n
2n
4n
n log n
quiz.explanation: A segment tree is a complete binary tree. For n leaves the tree has at most 2n nodes in the perfect case, but since n may not be a power of 2, the standard safe allocation is 4n nodes. The extra nodes are never used but prevent out-of-bounds indexing during build.

quiz.question: For a static array (no updates), which data structure achieves O(1) range minimum queries?
options: Segment tree — O(log n) query
Fenwick tree — O(log n) query
Sparse table — O(1) query using overlapping precomputed intervals
Sorted array — O(log n) via binary search
quiz.explanation: A sparse table precomputes minimum over every interval of length 2^k in O(n log n) time and O(n log n) space. For any query [l, r], two overlapping precomputed intervals cover it entirely — O(1) query. Because minimum is idempotent (min(a, a) = a), overlapping intervals do not double-count.

quiz.question: What is the time complexity to build a segment tree from an array of n elements?
options: O(log n)
O(n)
O(n log n)
quiz.explanation: Building fills all ~4n nodes of the tree. Each node is visited exactly once in a bottom-up traversal, performing O(1) work (combining two children). Total work is O(n) — the same as constructing a prefix-sum array.

quiz.question: In which real-world scenario would you use a segment tree with lazy propagation?
options: Building an autocomplete search feature over a dictionary
A leaderboard where individual scores change and you need the current top player
A game map where you need to add bonus damage to all enemies in a region, then query total health in another region
Sorting a list of transactions by timestamp
quiz.explanation: Range updates (add damage to a region) and range queries (total health in a region) are exactly the lazy-propagation use case. Without lazy propagation, a range update would visit every enemy individually — O(n). Lazy propagation defers the update, keeping both operations at O(log n).
